children: Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have withdrawn Rs 52,100 crore from Indian equities in October so far, as elevated crude oil prices, higher US bond yields and a stronger dollar weighed on investor sentiment.

The latest outflow comes after FPIs pulled out Rs 35,861 crore in September, according to data from the Central Depository Services (CDSL). Foreign investors had, however, invested Rs 20,200 crore in Indian equities in July and Rs 29,631 crore in August.

With the latest selling, cumulative FPI outflows from Indian equities in 2026 have reached Rs 3.12 trillion, significantly higher than the Rs 1.66 trillion withdrawn during the entire 2025, the data showed.
US Yields, Crude Weigh On Sentiment
Dheeraj Gaur, Chief Investment Strategy Officer at Choice Wealth, said FPIs have continued to sell Indian equities amid elevated US bond yields, a stronger dollar and rising crude oil prices.
Sticky US inflation has also increased expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike, making US assets relatively more attractive to global investors, he said.

At the same time, elevated crude oil prices are adding to economic pressures in India, while the artificial intelligence-led rally in North Asian markets is attracting foreign funds away from Indian equities, Gaur added.
However, foreign investors turned marginal buyers on 16 October, signalling a temporary reversal in the recent selling trend.

V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Investments Ltd, said the marginal decline in the US 10-year bond yield from above 5.3 per cent to 5.08 per cent, along with the rupee's strengthening against the dollar, were important factors behind the temporary change in FPI flows.

Sectorally, FPIs continued to sell shares of financial services and oil-related companies. However, they remained buyers in consumer services, including digital platform companies, entertainment, restaurants and healthcare services, Vijayakumar said.
Pabitro Mukherjee, Deputy Vice President-Research at Bajaj Broking, said the moderation in FPI selling and the reversal in flows on October 16 suggested that investor sentiment could be stabilising.
However, elevated crude oil prices remain a key risk to any sustained recovery in foreign investment flows, he said.

Going ahead, investors are likely to track Brent crude prices and developments in US-Iran relations, while domestic market attention will remain focused on second-quarter earnings for FY27, Mukherjee said.
Foreign investors also remained net sellers in India's debt market in September.
They withdrew Rs 1,620 crore through the Fully Accessible Route (FAR) and Rs 772 crore through the Voluntary Retention Route (VRR). However, they invested Rs 3,387 crore through the general route.

The continued foreign selling in Indian equities reflects the impact of global macroeconomic factors on capital flows, with US interest-rate expectations, currency movements, energy prices and geopolitical developments remaining key factors for investors.
